lessons.title: Logic, sets and relations
lessons.concept: Propositional logic combines statements using AND, OR, NOT and implication. P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false. First-order logic introduces predicates and quantifiers: ∀ means every element; ∃ means at least one. Negating a quantified statement swaps the quantifier and negates its predicate.
lessons.method: A relation is a subset of A × A. Reflexive, symmetric and transitive relations are equivalence relations and partition a set into disjoint classes. A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. A lattice has a unique greatest lower bound and least upper bound for every pair. Functions may be injective, surjective or bijective. A monoid has an associative operation and identity; a group additionally has an inverse for each element.
lessons.example: For three propositional variables a truth table has 2³ = 8 rows. On integers, aRb iff a − b is divisible by 3 is an equivalence relation with three equivalence classes. Distinguish antisymmetry from the absence of symmetry.

lessons.title: Graphs and combinatorics
lessons.concept: A graph consists of vertices and edges. Connectivity asks whether paths join vertices. A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoint. A proper colouring gives adjacent vertices different colours; a bipartite graph can be coloured with two colours iff it has no odd cycle.
lessons.method: Use the sum rule for disjoint choices and product rule for successive choices. Permutations count ordered selections n!/(n−r)!; combinations count unordered selections n!/[r!(n−r)!]. Inclusion–exclusion corrects overcounting. Recurrences describe a term using previous terms, and generating functions encode coefficients in a power series.
lessons.example: A tree on n vertices has n−1 edges. The number of ways to choose 3 vertices from 6 is 20. For aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ with a₀ = 1, aₙ = 2ⁿ and the generating function is 1/(1−2x).

lessons.title: Linear algebra
lessons.concept: Matrices represent linear transformations. Determinants identify whether a square matrix is invertible: det(A) ≠ 0 implies a unique solution to Ax = b. Row operations reveal rank and consistency. A system is consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A|b]).
lessons.method: An eigenvector v ≠ 0 satisfies Av = λv. Eigenvalues are roots of det(A−λI) = 0; their sum equals trace and product equals determinant. LU decomposition factors a matrix into lower and upper triangular factors, possibly requiring row pivoting, so repeated linear solves become efficient.
lessons.example: For A = diag(2,3), eigenvalues are 2 and 3 and determinant is 6. If a consistent system has n unknowns and rank r < n, there are n−r free variables. Do not confuse the number of equations with rank.

lessons.title: Calculus
lessons.concept: A limit describes the value approached near a point. Continuity at a requires lim f(x) = f(a). Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does not imply differentiability. A derivative measures local rate of change.
lessons.method: For interior extrema, inspect points where f′ is zero or undefined and compare endpoints on closed intervals. The mean value theorem requires continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b), then f′(c) = [f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a). Integration accumulates signed area; substitution and integration by parts simplify integrals.
lessons.example: For f(x)=x² on [0,2], the mean value theorem gives 2c=2, hence c=1. The integral from 0 to 2 is 8/3. For |x| at 0, continuity holds but differentiability fails.

lessons.title: Probability and statistics
lessons.concept: A random variable assigns numerical values to outcomes. Expectation is a probability-weighted average; variance is E[X²]−E[X]² and standard deviation is its square root. Median is a middle quantile; mode is the most frequent value.
lessons.method: Binomial(n,p) counts successes in independent trials: mean np, variance np(1−p). Poisson(λ) models counts with mean and variance λ. Uniform[a,b] has mean (a+b)/2. Exponential(λ) has mean 1/λ and is memoryless. Normal(μ,σ²) is symmetric around μ. Bayes: P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B).
lessons.example: For a fair coin tossed 4 times, P(exactly 2 heads)=6/16. If P(A)=0.2, P(B|A)=0.8 and P(B)=0.4, P(A|B)=0.4. Independence means P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), not that the events are disjoint.

name: Digital Logic
description: From Boolean expressions to working circuits

lessons.title: Boolean algebra and minimization
lessons.concept: Boolean variables take values 0 or 1. AND multiplies, OR adds logically, and NOT complements. De Morgan: ¬(AB)=¬A+¬B and ¬(A+B)=¬A¬B. Absorption gives A+AB=A.
lessons.method: Canonical sum-of-products lists minterms; product-of-sums lists maxterms. Karnaugh maps group adjacent 1s in powers of two, including wraparound adjacency, to eliminate changing variables. The tabular Quine–McCluskey method systematically combines minterms differing in one bit and selects prime implicants.
lessons.example: F=AB+A¬B simplifies to A. A four-cell K-map group in a 3-variable map eliminates two variables. Use don’t-care entries only when they improve the expression; they need not all be covered.

lessons.title: Combinational and sequential circuits
lessons.concept: Combinational outputs depend only on current inputs. Adders, multiplexers, decoders and encoders are typical examples. A full adder computes sum A⊕B⊕Cin and carry AB+ACin+BCin.
lessons.method: Sequential circuits retain state. Flip-flops sample at clock edges; latches are level sensitive. A D flip-flop has next state D, while a T flip-flop toggles when T=1. State tables and diagrams guide counter and finite-state machine design. Respect setup and hold constraints.
lessons.example: A 4:1 multiplexer needs two select lines. A binary counter with k flip-flops has up to 2ᵏ states. Moore outputs depend on state; Mealy outputs depend on state and current input.

lessons.title: Number representation and arithmetic
lessons.concept: Unsigned n-bit values range from 0 to 2ⁿ−1. Two’s complement values range from −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹−1; negate by inverting bits and adding one. Fixed point reserves a fixed number of fractional bits.
lessons.method: Floating point represents sign × significand × base^exponent. IEEE 754 single precision uses 1 sign, 8 exponent and 23 stored fraction bits, with exponent bias 127 for normal values. Floating-point arithmetic rounds, and addition may lose smaller terms. Signed overflow occurs when same-sign addition produces the opposite sign.
lessons.example: In 8-bit two’s complement, −5 is 11111011. With four fractional bits, stored integer 24 represents 1.5. Distinguish carry-out, which concerns unsigned overflow, from signed overflow.

name: Computer Organization
description: Understand what happens beneath your code

lessons.title: Instructions, addressing and control
lessons.concept: An instruction identifies an operation and operands. Immediate addressing supplies a literal; direct addressing supplies a memory address; register indirect uses a register holding an address. Indexed and base-relative modes compute effective addresses.
lessons.method: An ALU implements arithmetic and bitwise operations, with flags for carry, zero, sign and overflow. Hardwired control uses logic to generate signals; microprogrammed control reads microinstructions from a control store. CPU time = instruction count × CPI × clock cycle time.
lessons.example: If 10⁶ instructions have CPI 2 on a 1 GHz CPU, execution time is 2 ms. For base 1000 and displacement 24, the effective address is 1024. A faster clock does not alone guarantee less execution time.

lessons.title: Memory, caches and I/O
lessons.concept: The hierarchy trades speed against capacity: registers, caches, main memory and storage. Temporal locality reuses recent data; spatial locality accesses nearby data. Direct mapping assigns a block to one line; set associativity permits several lines in one set.
lessons.method: Address bits divide into tag, index and offset. Average memory access time is hit time + miss rate × miss penalty for a single cache. Memory interfacing uses address decoding and control signals. Interrupt-driven I/O notifies the CPU; DMA transfers blocks with little CPU intervention.
lessons.example: A 32-bit address, 64-byte block and 256 direct-mapped lines uses 6 offset bits, 8 index bits and 18 tag bits. With hit time 1 ns, miss rate 0.05 and penalty 40 ns, AMAT is 3 ns.

lessons.title: Pipelining and hazards
lessons.concept: Pipelining overlaps instruction stages. For k equal stages and n instructions, ideal cycles are k+n−1; a pipeline improves throughput, while individual instruction latency still includes every stage.
lessons.method: Structural hazards compete for hardware; data hazards arise from dependencies; control hazards come from branches. Forwarding can resolve many read-after-write dependencies, but load-use dependencies may still stall. Branch prediction reduces control penalties and wrong predictions require flushing.
lessons.example: A 5-stage pipeline running 10 instructions ideally takes 14 cycles. Always add actual stalls and flush penalties. A dependency does not automatically imply a stall if the needed data can be forwarded in time.

name: Programming & Data Structures
description: Build a strong foundation in C and structures

lessons.title: C programming and recursion
lessons.concept: C uses typed variables, pointers and explicit memory management. Arrays usually decay to pointers in expressions, but sizeof an actual array measures its full storage. Pointer arithmetic advances in units of the pointed-to type.
lessons.method: A recursive function needs a base case and progress toward it. Each active call has its own stack frame. Pass-by-value copies arguments; passing a pointer allows modifying the pointed-to object. Avoid undefined behaviour such as out-of-bounds access, dangling pointers and unsequenced modifications.
lessons.example: For int a[5], sizeof(a)=5×sizeof(int) where a is an array in scope. In a function parameter int a[], a is adjusted to a pointer. Factorial recursion takes O(n) time and O(n) stack space.

lessons.title: Arrays, lists, stacks and queues
lessons.concept: Arrays support O(1) indexed access and O(n) middle insertion. Linked lists store nodes connected by pointers; insertion after a known node is O(1), while searching is O(n).
lessons.method: A stack is last-in-first-out and supports expression evaluation and DFS. A queue is first-in-first-out and supports BFS. Circular queues reuse array space and distinguish full and empty using a count or an unused slot. A doubly linked list permits backward traversal.
lessons.example: Pushing 1, 2, 3 and popping twice produces 3 then 2. Enqueuing the same values and dequeuing twice produces 1 then 2. Account for traversal time when a list insertion position is not already known.

lessons.title: Trees, heaps and graph representations
lessons.concept: A binary search tree stores smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right; inorder traversal produces sorted order. Operations take O(h), where h is height, and can degrade to O(n).
lessons.method: A binary heap is a complete binary tree with heap order. In a zero-based array, children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2. Heap insertion and root removal cost O(log n), while bottom-up heap construction is O(n). Graph adjacency lists use O(V+E) space; matrices use O(V²).
lessons.example: A min-heap guarantees the minimum at its root but does not sort every level. A BST formed by inserting ascending keys can become a chain. Adjacency lists are effective for sparse graphs.

name: Algorithms
description: Learn to choose, prove and analyze algorithms

lessons.title: Complexity, searching, sorting and hashing
lessons.concept: Big-O gives an asymptotic upper bound; Ω gives a lower bound and Θ a tight bound. Include auxiliary space separately from input storage. Binary search on sorted data takes O(log n); linear search takes O(n).
lessons.method: Merge sort is Θ(n log n) with O(n) auxiliary array space. Quicksort is expected O(n log n) but worst-case O(n²). Heapsort has O(n log n) worst-case time. Hashing supports expected O(1) operations under appropriate assumptions; collisions are handled by chaining or probing.
lessons.example: The recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+n yields Θ(n log n). Comparison sorting requires Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. A hash table with a high load factor may have long chains or probing sequences.

lessons.title: Greedy, dynamic programming and divide-and-conquer
lessons.concept: Divide-and-conquer splits independent subproblems and combines results. Greedy algorithms commit to locally optimal choices; correctness generally needs an exchange argument or a structural property.
lessons.method: Dynamic programming stores results of overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure. Define the state, transition, base cases and evaluation order before coding. For 0/1 knapsack, dp[i,w] compares skipping item i with including it when its weight fits.
lessons.example: Activity selection by earliest finishing time is optimal. Greedy choice by value-to-weight ratio solves fractional knapsack but can fail for 0/1 knapsack. Fibonacci with memoization takes O(n) time instead of exponential recursion.

lessons.title: Graph traversal, spanning trees and shortest paths
lessons.concept: BFS explores layers and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. DFS explores deeply and helps with cycle detection and topological ordering. Both take O(V+E) using adjacency lists.
lessons.method: Kruskal selects increasing-weight edges avoiding cycles; Prim grows a tree from a starting vertex. Dijkstra requires nonnegative edges; Bellman–Ford handles negative edges and detects reachable negative cycles. Floyd–Warshall finds all-pairs shortest paths in O(V³).
lessons.example: An MST in a connected graph on n vertices uses n−1 edges. An MST minimizes total tree weight, not every source-to-vertex path. Dijkstra’s greedy finalization can fail when an edge has negative weight.

lessons.title: Regular languages and finite automata
lessons.concept: A DFA has exactly one transition per state and input symbol; an NFA may have several or epsilon transitions. Both recognize exactly the regular languages. Subset construction converts an NFA to a DFA, potentially using 2ⁿ states.
lessons.method: Regular expressions use union, concatenation and Kleene star. Regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement and concatenation. DFA minimization merges states that no suffix can distinguish. A DFA cannot count arbitrary matched quantities.
lessons.example: The expression (0|1)*01 denotes strings ending in 01. The language {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n≥0} is not regular. To complement a DFA, first make transitions total and then swap accepting and nonaccepting states.

lessons.title: Context-free languages, grammars and pumping
lessons.concept: A context-free grammar replaces a single nonterminal with a string. Push-down automata add a stack and recognize context-free languages. Derivations produce parse trees; ambiguity means one string has multiple parse trees.
lessons.method: Regular pumping: sufficiently long strings split xyz with |xy|≤p and |y|>0, and xyⁱz remains in the language for every i≥0. Context-free pumping uses uvxyz with |vxy|≤p and |vy|>0, pumping v and y together. These lemmas prove nonmembership, not generally membership.
lessons.example: S → 0S1 | ε generates {0ⁿ1ⁿ}. CFLs are closed under union and concatenation, but not general intersection or complement. For a pumping proof, handle every allowed decomposition chosen by the opponent.

lessons.title: Turing machines and undecidability
lessons.concept: A Turing machine has finite control and an unbounded tape. A decider halts on every input; a recognizer may run forever on inputs outside its language. Every decidable language is recognizable, but the converse fails.
lessons.method: The halting problem is undecidable. Reductions transfer difficulty: to prove B undecidable, transform a known undecidable problem A into B. Rice’s theorem concerns every nontrivial semantic property of the language recognized by a Turing machine.
lessons.example: If both a language and its complement are recognizable, run the recognizers in interleaved steps; one accepts and you obtain a decider. Rice’s theorem does not directly apply to purely syntactic properties such as the number of states.

name: Compiler Design
description: Follow a program from source to execution

lessons.title: Lexical analysis and parsing
lessons.concept: Lexical analysis groups characters into tokens, often with regular expressions and finite automata. Parsing checks token sequences against a context-free grammar and constructs a parse tree.
lessons.method: Top-down LL parsing builds a leftmost derivation; bottom-up LR parsing reconstructs a rightmost derivation in reverse. FIRST describes possible initial terminals and FOLLOW describes terminals after a nonterminal. LL(1) tables must have no conflicting entries. Left recursion prevents ordinary recursive-descent parsing.
lessons.example: For E → TE′ and E′ → +TE′ | ε, FIRST(E′) contains + and ε. Populate epsilon-production entries using FOLLOW. Distinguish a lexical error from a syntactically invalid token sequence.

lessons.title: Translation, runtime and intermediate code
lessons.concept: Syntax-directed translation associates attributes or actions with grammar rules. Synthesized attributes flow from children to parents; inherited attributes receive context from parents or siblings.
lessons.method: Runtime activation records hold parameters, return information, saved state and local variables. Three-address code breaks expressions into simple operations. Intermediate representations enable machine-independent optimization; backpatching resolves forward jump targets.
lessons.example: For a=b+c*d, emit t1=c*d, t2=b+t1, a=t2. Operator precedence makes multiplication happen first. Recursive calls require separate activation records to preserve distinct local variables.

lessons.title: Optimization and data flow
lessons.concept: Local optimization operates within a basic block. Constant propagation replaces variables known to have constant values. Common-subexpression elimination reuses an earlier computed expression if its operands have not changed.
lessons.method: Liveness is backward analysis: OUT[B] is the union of successor IN sets, and IN[B]=USE[B] ∪ (OUT[B]−DEF[B]). Iteration continues to a fixed point. Available expressions are a forward analysis whose merge generally uses intersection.
lessons.example: In x=4; y=x+2, propagation lets y become 6. In t=a+b; a=0; u=a+b, the second expression cannot reuse t because a changed. A value is live only if some path uses it before redefining it.

name: Operating System
description: Processes, memory and the systems between them

lessons.title: Processes, threads and synchronization
lessons.concept: A process owns an address space and resources; threads within it share these but have separate stacks and registers. System calls enter the kernel for protected operations. IPC includes pipes, messages and shared memory.
lessons.method: Concurrent operations can race when outcomes depend on interleaving. A critical section protects shared state. Mutexes enforce mutual exclusion; semaphores support counting and signaling. Correct protocols need mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting under their assumptions.
lessons.example: Two unsynchronized increments of a shared variable can lose an update because read-modify-write is not atomic. A counting semaphore initialized to k can control access to k identical resources.

lessons.title: Deadlock and scheduling
lessons.concept: Deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait. Prevention breaks a condition; avoidance checks whether a safe completion sequence remains; detection identifies deadlock after it occurs.
lessons.method: FCFS may cause a convoy effect; SJF minimizes mean waiting time under known bursts for simultaneous arrivals; round-robin trades responsiveness against switching overhead. Turnaround=completion−arrival, waiting=turnaround−CPU burst. I/O scheduling includes FCFS, SSTF and SCAN.
lessons.example: For simultaneous CPU bursts 3 and 5 scheduled in that order, waiting times are 0 and 3, mean 1.5. An unsafe state is not necessarily already deadlocked. Banker’s algorithm reasons about maximum future demands.

lessons.title: Memory, virtual memory and files
lessons.concept: Paging maps virtual pages to physical frames using page tables; a TLB caches translations. Page offset stays unchanged by translation. Demand paging loads pages when referenced, potentially producing a page fault.
lessons.method: FIFO, LRU and optimal replacement choose victims differently; FIFO can show Belady’s anomaly. Working sets describe actively used pages; insufficient frames can cause thrashing. File systems organize names, metadata and blocks using contiguous, linked or indexed allocation.
lessons.example: A 4 KiB page has a 12-bit offset. A 32-bit virtual address therefore has 20 page-number bits. A TLB miss is not necessarily a page fault: the page may already be in physical memory.

name: Databases
description: Model, query and protect your data

lessons.title: ER, relational model and queries
lessons.concept: ER modeling identifies entities, attributes and relationships with cardinality constraints. Relations store tuples under a schema. Keys uniquely identify tuples; foreign keys connect relations and enforce referential integrity.
lessons.method: Relational algebra combines selection, projection, joins, union and difference. Tuple calculus describes desired tuples declaratively. SQL uses SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING; WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups. SQL generally keeps duplicates unless DISTINCT is used.
lessons.example: SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM student GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 returns departments with more than five rows. Relational algebra projection eliminates duplicates, whereas a basic SQL SELECT does not.

lessons.title: Dependencies, constraints and normal forms
lessons.concept: A functional dependency X→Y means equal X values require equal Y values. Attribute closure finds what a set determines and helps identify candidate keys. Integrity constraints include domain, entity and referential constraints.
lessons.method: 2NF eliminates partial dependence of nonprime attributes on a candidate key. 3NF requires for each nontrivial X→A that X is a superkey or A is prime. BCNF requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey. Decomposition should be lossless; dependency preservation is an additional desirable property.
lessons.example: For R(A,B,C) with A→B and B→C, A is a key and B→C violates BCNF. Decomposing into AB and BC is lossless. Do not infer dependencies from a small sample table alone.

lessons.title: Indexing, transactions and concurrency
lessons.concept: File organization influences lookup and scan cost. B-trees are balanced search trees; B+ trees store data entries at leaves and link leaves for efficient range scans. Index fanout reduces the number of disk levels.
lessons.method: Transactions aim for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. Conflict serializability holds iff the precedence graph is acyclic. Two-phase locking separates acquiring and releasing locks; it can deadlock. Recovery uses logs and appropriate write-ahead rules.
lessons.example: If T1 writes X before T2 reads X, add edge T1→T2. A cycle means the schedule is not conflict serializable. A B+ tree supports ordered range scans efficiently, while hashing primarily targets equality lookups.

lessons.title: Layering, switching and performance
lessons.concept: Layers separate responsibilities and expose services to the layer above. Encapsulation adds headers. Circuit switching reserves a path; packet switching shares links, while virtual circuits establish a logical route before forwarding packets.
lessons.method: Transmission delay=L/R, propagation delay=distance/speed. Queueing depends on load; processing adds device overhead. End-to-end store-and-forward delay includes transmission at every link, with pipelining for multiple packets.
lessons.example: A 1000-byte packet on an 8 Mbps link takes 1 ms to transmit. Propagation over 2000 km at 2×10⁸ m/s takes 10 ms. Increasing bandwidth reduces transmission delay, not propagation delay.

lessons.title: Data link, Ethernet and routing
lessons.concept: Error detection uses parity, checksums or CRC. CRC treats bit strings as polynomials over GF(2) and appends a division remainder. Medium access controls sharing; classic half-duplex Ethernet uses CSMA/CD.
lessons.method: Switches learn source MAC addresses and forward by destination. Distance-vector routing exchanges distance estimates with neighbors; link-state routing floods topology information and computes shortest paths. Distance-vector protocols can suffer count-to-infinity.
lessons.example: A generator polynomial of degree r produces r CRC bits. Modern full-duplex switched Ethernet does not use collision detection. Link-state routing uses Dijkstra on the known topology.

lessons.title: IPv4, CIDR, fragmentation and NAT
lessons.concept: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses. A /p prefix leaves 32−p host bits; subnet masking identifies the network. Longest-prefix match chooses the most specific matching route. NAT translates addresses, often ports too.
lessons.method: Fragmentation divides an IP datagram to fit an MTU. Fragment offsets are in 8-byte units and all nonfinal fragment payloads must be multiples of eight. Account for the header on each fragment. The more-fragments flag is zero only for the final fragment.
lessons.example: A /26 subnet contains 64 addresses, usually 62 assignable host addresses. A 4000-byte datagram with 20-byte header and MTU 1500 has payload pieces 1480,1480,1020 with offsets 0,185,370.

lessons.title: TCP, sockets, DNS and HTTP
lessons.concept: TCP provides reliable ordered byte delivery with acknowledgments and retransmissions. Flow control protects the receiver using its advertised window; congestion control protects the network using a congestion window. The sending limit depends on both.
lessons.method: Slow start increases congestion window rapidly; congestion avoidance increases more slowly. Sockets expose operations such as bind, listen, accept and connect. DNS resolves names using caches and hierarchical servers. HTTP defines request/response semantics; persistent connections reuse transport connections.
lessons.example: If receiver window is 16 KiB and congestion window is 8 KiB, the usable window is at most 8 KiB before accounting for outstanding data. DNS commonly uses UDP but also TCP. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.

name: General Aptitude
description: Extra exam practice beyond your CS PDF

lessons.title: Verbal, quantitative and analytical aptitude
lessons.concept: Verbal aptitude tests grammar, vocabulary and comprehension. Read the exact claim in a passage and avoid replacing it with outside assumptions. Quantitative questions require translating words into equations and tracking units.
lessons.method: Percent change=(new−old)/old×100. Average=total/count. Work rates add when workers work simultaneously. Analytical reasoning uses constraints, arrangements and elimination. Spatial aptitude asks you to reason about rotation, reflection and shapes.
lessons.example: A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease gives 1.2×0.8=0.96, a net 4% decrease. If A completes a task in 6 days and B in 3, together they finish in 2 days.
